title: A Book as Big as the War

Review

A Book as Big as the War

‘1942’ offers an epic, brilliant vision of global conflict.

August 28, 2026, 3:00 PM

By Keith Johnson, a staff writer at Foreign Policy covering geoeconomics and energy.

Geopolitics

World War II books have a habit of being as enormous as the conflict itself. The average war buff owns at least a couple of hefty tomes that could, in a pinch, stop a bullet or two, whether it’s Gerhard Weinberg’s classic A World at Arms (1,208 pages), Richard Overy’s Blood and Ruins (1,040 pages), or Antony Beevor’s The Second World War (880 pages). Even a relatively svelte volume like John Ellis’ One Day In a Very Long War runs over 400 pages. The third world war could be fought by using World War II books as artillery shells.
Jonathan Parshall’s 1942: Crux of War is a 17-year labor of love—as well as dogged perseverance and inveterate curiosity—that, at 1,280 pages, can easily hold its own among the big boys. The book is a sprawling, blow-by-blow account of a single year, but one that was the linchpin of everything to follow. As Parshall notes, 1942 encompassed the crux of the entire war—12 months in which everything started out catastrophically for the Allies and (nearly) ended up swimmingly. That was the year that featured the battles of Midway, Guadalcanal, El Alamein, and Stalingrad, all of them crushing victories for the anti-fascist coalition.

Jonathan Parshall’s 1942: Crux of War is a 17-year labor of love—as well as dogged perseverance and inveterate curiosity—that, at 1,280 pages, can easily hold its own among the big boys. The book is a sprawling, blow-by-blow account of a single year, but one that was the linchpin of everything to follow. As Parshall notes, 1942 encompassed the crux of the entire war—12 months in which everything started out catastrophically for the Allies and (nearly) ended up swimmingly. That was the year that featured the battles of Midway, Guadalcanal, El Alamein, and Stalingrad, all of them crushing victories for the anti-fascist coalition.
As Winston Churchill said after British church bells rang for the first time after victory at El Alamein in November 1942, “This is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning.”
Parshall tells the story of every action in every theater of war with careful detail and an eye to answering the question, how did we get here from there? The biggest virtue of Parshall’s book is that he can write empathically from the viewpoint of the time, not with the benefit of eight decades of hindsight. It’s easy, if discomfiting, to look back on the rebar remains of Hiroshima or on bombed-out Berlin and believe that Allied victory in World War II was a foregone conclusion. But as Parshall stresses throughout, “It sure wasn’t obvious at the time.”

Black and white photo of a large formation of soldiers standing in ranks with rifles held upright on a grassy hillside.
Japanese troops present arms as they amass on the Indochina-Burmese border circa 1942. Keystone/Getty Images

There are probably a million books on World War II, catering to every taste and fancy. There are books on single battles, or extended campaigns. There are one-volume histories, two-volume couplets, and some lovely trilogies. There are wonderful books on the naval war, the strategic bombing campaign, and the Battle of the Atlantic, from both sides. There are books focused on economics, war production, and even food. And memoirs galore, of course.

What makes Parshall’s book special is his ability to tell the story of the whole war at a time when the conflict still seemed to hang in the balance. The first three years of the war were an unmitigated disaster for the Allies, from Poland to Norway, France, the Low Countries, the Balkans, Greece, and North Africa. Then came the invasion of Russia, the mass surrender of Soviet forces, and the Germans at the gates of Moscow—plus the U-boat offensive in the Atlantic. And then it got worse.
The Japanese attack on U.S. Pacific possessions at Pearl Harbor and the Philippines, coupled with a lightning attack on British colonies in Hong Kong and Malaya, were hammer blows both to the troops on the ground and, above all, the leaders in London. When British forces in Singapore, Britain’s greatest fortress, fell to an invading Japanese army with one-third as many men in early 1942, Britain’s warlords were despairing.
The head of the British Army, “General [Alan] Brooke confided to his diary that he ‘certainly never expected that we should fall to pieces as fast as we are, and to see Hong Kong and Singapore go in less than three months plus a failure in the Western Desert is far from reassuring.’ Noting Britain’s previous powers of recovery, he wondered ‘whether we shall again bring off a comeback?,’” Parshall writes.

Black and white photograph of an official inspecting two opposing rows of uniformed soldiers holding rifles, set outdoors near a vessel or dock structure.
British Prime Minister Winston Churchill inspects troops in December 1942. Fox Photos/Hulton Archive/Getty Images)
The comeback that they did pull off—the British as well as the Americans and the Soviets—make up the rest of the 1,200-odd pages of this very thorough and thoroughly enjoyable book.
Parshall cracks his knuckles and sets to work with a month-by-month chronicle of the crucial year, with a detailed analysis of every theater of war. There is a lot of old-school military history (Parshall’s vocation by training) with corps, divisions, and brigades marching over maps or holding river lines. Woe betides the reader who confuses the 22nd Panzer with the 24th Panzer or the Australian 7th Division with the British 7th Armoured Brigade.

The Irresistible Urge to Invoke World War III

Forget the inflated comparisons. Neither the war in the Middle East nor the Russian invasion of Ukraine ever signaled a global conflagration.

Analysis
|

Jo Inge Bekkevold

To his credit, for a historian who was weaned to his craft by a fascination with the Pacific theater, and whose previous great work was on its pivotal battle, Parshall gives every theater its due—even if there are plenty of cruiser-on-cruiser battles and a good few pages on the Battle of Midway.
But the beauty of Parshall’s book lies elsewhere.

Black and white painting showing a damaged military aircraft sitting on open ground under a dramatic, cloudy sky, with figures standing near the cockpit.
An official war painting by Capt. Peter McIntyre depicts British military personnel guarding a crashed Stuka, a German attack bomber, during the North African campaign in Libya, circa 1942. Captain Peter McIntyre/European/FPG/Archive Photos/Getty Images

Parshall prefaces each monthly bulletin with a big-picture essay; taken together, these would make for a great book in their own right. They range from detailed analyses of the economics of tank or aircraft production, to the difficulties the United States faced in mobilizing slack industrial capacity for total war; from managing a cumbersome U.S.-U.K. command system, to the transformation of the Red Army from cannon fodder to deep battle specialists.

Parshall ties all the theaters of war together in a way largely unparalleled in World War II history. He offers a vision that is certainly lost in narrow biographies of battles, but which also fails to cohere even in the best supposedly comprehensive histories.
To pluck one example at random: When, on a lark in the spring of 1942, the Imperial Japanese Navy launched a nonsensical raid into the Indian Ocean and raised havoc with British naval forces and merchant shipping, the Royal Navy’s response was to leave a strong naval force in East Africa. That starved the already-beleaguered Mediterranean Fleet of ships precisely at a time when it was actually losing the naval war against Italy, which had nasty implications for the war in North Africa, as Gen. Erwin Rommel and Germany’s Afrika Korps nearly took Egypt.
For a book about events 80-some years ago, there sure is a lot of suspense. That takes us back to Parshall’s original point: For the statesmen, generals, soldiers, sailors, and airmen of the time, there was a lot of suspense. Victory was a slogan, not a given. There was nothing deterministic about it.
I think this might be my desert island book—and not just because, in a pinch, it could be a serviceable shelter.
